developments in water leakage management for water supply systems

A B S T R A C T
Detecting water leakage represents a significant and pervasive challenge in water supply systems due to the 
complexity of network behavior, and the diversity of leakage manifestations, which may remain undetected. 
The magnitude of leakage varies considerably, from 3% to over 50%, depending on the level of maintenance 
undertaken. The global volume of water loss per year is estimated to be 126 billion cubic meters, equivalent 
to a financial loss of over 30 billion USD. To address this problem, leakage management strategies have been 
developed, including preventive measures, systematic assessment protocols, regulatory frameworks, stringent 
control measures, detection and localization techniques, and prompt repair initiatives. The detection and 
localization phase is particularly important due to its inherent complexity and critical role, where various 
techniques are used, including hardware- and software-based, and hybrid methods. These techniques include 
the implementation of Machine Learning models that provide an advantage in automated data analysis, leading 
to faster detection and localization of leakage in water supply systems. Moreover, commercial solutions and 
patented technologies are continuing to converge into more integrated and scalable monitoring strategies.
This paper presents a state-of-the-art review of scientific, commercial, and industrial developments in 
water leakage management for water supply systems. The scientific review provides a critical and integrative 
comparison of existing methodologies, highlighting the trade-offs regarding practical applicability, including 
scalability, data dependency, uncertainty propagation, and localization accuracy. Additionally, Machine Learn-
ing applications to this field, as well as leak detection and localization performance indicators, are presented. A 
focused analysis of the BattLeDIM competition highlights leading methodologies and underlines the potential of 
hybrid approaches that merge hydraulic modeling with advanced analytics. Furthermore, the commercial and 
industrial analysis provides valuable insights into the main technologies and techniques employed by leading 
companies, and the current status of registered patents regarding water leakage detection and localization, 
highlighting interesting trends. Overall, this review bridges scientific, commercial, and industrial knowledge 
across sectors and highlights key priorities for advancing scalable and operationally robust leakage detection 
strategies.

1. Introduction
According to the International Water Association (IWA) in the Stan-
dard Definition of Water Losses (Pearson, 2019), the Water Supply 
Systems (WSS) volume of treated water is categorized as authorized 
consumption (billed and unbilled consumption) and water losses (ap-
parent and real losses), as illustrated in Fig. 1. The apparent losses, 
also called commercial losses, include unauthorized consumption and 
inaccuracies in metering and billing. On the other hand, real losses are 
physical losses that include water leakage, taking place in pipes and/or 
junctions with uncontrolled actions (Liemberger and Wyatt, 2019; Wan 
et al., 2022) and can remain undetected for long periods without an 
effective detection and solution (Negm et al., 2023).
The global demand for water is expected to increase by 40% by 
2030 (European Commission, 2024), with the European Commission 
establishing a target of at least a 10% improvement in water effi-
ciency (European Environment Agency, 2025). Despite these efforts, 
water losses remain a major global challenge. Current estimates indi-
cate that between 30%–35% of supplied water is lost worldwide (Al-
saydalani, 2024; IDRICA, 2024; Khaled, 2025). According to the World 
Bank’s global water monitoring report (Editorial Team SDG6, 2024), 
this is estimated to correspond to approximately 126 billion cubic me-
ters per year, equivalent to 324–346 million cubic meters per day (Ed-
itorial Team SDG6, 2024; World Bank Media, 2025; Liemberger and 
Wyatt, 2019; Komy, 2025; Alsaydalani, 2024; Pathirane et al., 2024; 
IDRICA, 2024). If this volume were reduced by one third, it would still 
be sufficient to supply water to more than 800 million people, assuming 
a daily per capita consumption of 150 liters (Liemberger and Wyatt, 
2019).
Water loss due to leakage is strongly influenced by the time elapsed 
between leak occurrence and detection (Bakker et al., 2014; Z. Hu 
et al., 2021). In well-maintained systems, losses typically range from 
3%–7% (Beuken et al., 2008; Puust et al., 2010), whereas 20%–30% 
are observed in moderately maintained systems (El-Zahab and Zayed, 
2019). In poorly maintained systems and in developing countries, water 
losses can exceed 50% (Lambert, 2002; Puust et al., 2010; Alsaydalani, 
2024).
Despite the global scale of the problem, several countries demon-
strate that high efficiency and low water loss levels are achievable. 
For instance, water losses are reported to be below 4% in the Nether-
lands (SPML - Engineering Life, 2022), and approximately 5% in Sin-
gapore (Khaled, 2025). Similarly, countries such as Germany, Den-
mark, Japan, Australia, and Israel report relatively low loss rates of 
6%–10% (We Are Water - Foundation, 2024; SPML - Engineering Life, 
2022). These examples highlight the effectiveness of investment in 
infrastructure maintenance, monitoring, and leakage control.
In contrast, water losses across Europe remain comparatively high, 
with an estimated 23%–26% of water lost during the distribution 
process due to leaking pipes and inadequate infrastructure (European 
Commission, 2024; AVK Non-Revenue Water Solutions, 2017). Some 
countries still perform better than the European average, including 
Austria (with losses below 15%) (European Environment Agency, 2025) 
and the Czech Republic (with losses under 20%) (SPML - Engineering 
Life, 2022). However, in several other European countries, including 
Bulgaria, Croatia, and Italy, water losses can exceed 40% (European 
Environment Agency, 2025). Recent findings show that the implemen-
tation of mitigation measures can substantially reduce leakage rates. 
For example, Ireland reduced water losses from 46% in 2018 to 3% 
in 2021, as part of efforts to achieve the EU’s target of 25% by 
2023 (European Environment Agency, 2025). In Portugal, the regu-
latory authority ERSAR (ERSAR, 2023) reported that, in 2023, water 
losses were 5.6 m3∕(km day) on the bulk side and 2.4 m3∕(km day) in the 
distribution network, corresponding to approximately 184 million liters 
per year.
In the USA, water losses are estimated at approximately 16%
(Khaled, 2025), which might correspond to nearly 8 trillion liters per 
year, largely due to ageing infrastructure (SPML - Engineering Life, 
2022). Significantly higher losses are reported in many regions of 
Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and South America, where water loss 
can often exceed 50% (Alsaydalani, 2024; Khaled, 2025). Particularly 
severe cases include Nigeria and India, where losses can reach up to 
65% (We Are Water - Foundation, 2024; SPML - Engineering Life, 
2022), followed by Iraq and Haiti, with losses of up to 60% (We Are 
Water - Foundation, 2024; IDRICA, 2024; Khaled, 2025). Furthermore, 
cities and countries such as Mexico City, Jordan, Lebanon, South 
Africa, Algeria, Palestine, and Sri Lanka report losses in the range of 
40%–50% (We Are Water - Foundation, 2024; IDRICA, 2024; Khaled, 
2025; SPML - Engineering Life, 2022; Pathirane et al., 2024), while 
Egypt and Brazil exhibit approximately 34%–38% of water lost (SPML 
- Engineering Life, 2022; IDRICA, 2024).
Water leakage can be divided according to the amount of water 
that is lost into reported or unreported leaks. Reported leaks are also 
known as burst leaks with a high flow visible above the ground, which 
are quickly detected and repaired. Unreported leaks represent the most 
significant amount of leakage, causing more damage. These leaks are 
‘‘invisible’’, with a moderate flow, and can remain undetected for a few 
days or weeks. On the other hand, the unreported background leaks are 
dependent on the infrastructure conditions, since they happen through 
fittings, small cracks or joints (Lambert, 1994; Wan et al., 2022; Negm 
et al., 2023; Lopez et al., 2025; Barros et al., 2024).
Leak detection is a challenging problem due to the complexity of 
WSS networks. They include different consumption locations, source 
points, and pipe infrastructure conditions. These infrastructure condi-
tions rely on different pipe materials, diameters, age-related internal or 
external corrosion and deterioration, inadequate fittings, among oth-
ers (Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020; Barton et al., 2019) which 
can lead to possible periodic pipe failure (Zaman et al., 2020; Lopez 
et al., 2025). In addition, leaks can be caused by other factors such 
as mechanical damage caused by excessive pipe loading, high system 
pressure, pipe defects, temperature variations, ground movement or 
excavation damage, soil conditions and poor workmanship (Puust et al., 
2010; Lopez et al., 2025). These leaks originate from minor weaknesses 
points in the pipes and evolve into cracks due to pressure fatigue and 
corrosion. The occurrence of a leak is typically preceded by the creation 
of a physical opening in the pipe wall, which subsequently results in 
the leakage. Consequently, the process of growth commences until the 
external manifestation is apparent (Lopez et al., 2025).

To try to minimize the occurrence of leaks, leakage management 
measures can be implemented, such as identifying problematic pipes 
and water audits. These measures include the detection and localization 
step, which is one of the most complex steps of the process and where 
a multitude of techniques and approaches can be applied to try to 
solve it (Wan et al., 2022; Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020). 
The two most widespread methods are the hardware-based and the 
software-based. Hardware-based methods are known for needing a 
physical device to search for leaks. On the other hand, software-based 
methods rely on data analysis and hydraulic models, where Machine 
Learning (ML) techniques can positively impact quicker leakage detec-
tion and localization. ML can process large amounts of information to 
perform tasks without explicit instructions. It obtains good results for 
(1) different data labeling conditions (supervised, unsupervised, semi-
supervised, and reinforcement learning) (Mota et al., 2025; Brunton 
and Kutz, 2017; Géron, 2019; Sutton and Barto, 2014; Bhattacharya 
et al., 2003), (2) different learning approaches (incremental and batch 
learning) (Ma et al., 2020; Losing et al., 2018; Géron, 2019), (3) 
different approaches for data point comparison (instance-based and 
model-based) (Shlezinger et al., 2021; Taser et al., 2019). Therefore, 
quantitative and qualitative metrics must be defined to evaluate the 
effectiveness of the applied methods.
Building on previous research, this study conducts a revision on 
three key branches of water leakage detection and localization analysis. 
First, it presents a scientific review of methodologies discussed in the 
current literature for detecting and localizing water leaks, providing 
a classification of these methods and approaches. It also presents ML 
applications in the WSS area and some performance indicators to 
evaluate the effectiveness of these methodologies. Additionally, the 
benchmark case study of BattLeDIM is shown to demonstrate how 
the previous methodologies are applied. Following, and to the best of 
the authors’ knowledge, this work introduces two novel perspectives: 
a review of commercial and industrial applications, highlighting the 
primary technologies employed by leading companies, as well as an 
analysis of registered patents related to water leakage detection and 
localization.
The document is structured into the following sections: Section 2 
‘‘Research Methodology’’ presents the research methodology employed 
in this study, delineating the path across the scientific, commercial, 
and industrial reviews. Section 3 ‘‘Scientific Review: Water Leakage 
Detection and Localization’’ provides a brief overview of the various 
leakage management measures that can be implemented to reduce 
water losses and categorizes different techniques for the detection and 
localization phase, describing the detection process and data process-
ing. It summarizes the hardware-based and software-based methods, 
explaining the model-based, data-driven and hybrid techniques. This 
section also discusses the application of ML techniques to WSS, which 
are increasingly used within data-driven and hybrid leakage detection 
frameworks and presents the most common performance indicators for 
leakage detection and localization approaches. A practical application 
and benchmarking of the BattLeDIM case study are also presented in 
this section. Section 4 ‘‘Commercial Review: Company Technologies’’ 
outlines the commercial application of the technologies used for wa-
ter leak detection and localization, summarizing the main companies 
involved and main case studies where the technology was applied. 
Section 5 ‘‘Industrial Review: Registered Patents’’ provides an industrial 
review of registered patents worldwide, examining their percentage 
distribution based on the methodologies employed. Additionally, it 
analyzes the annual trends of granted patents, categorized by the type 
of methodology utilized. Finally, Section 6 ‘‘Conclusions and Future Re-
search Direction’’ showcases this work’s main conclusions and findings, 
alongside future research directions.
2. Research methodology
Fig. 2 illustrates the research methodology adopted in this work. 
The scientific review focused on highly cited research papers on water 
leakage detection and localization methodologies, specifically software-
based techniques, which have gained increasing relevance due to their 
growing prevalence and continuous development and adoption. The 
selected papers provide a comprehensive analysis of the definitions, 
concepts, and methodologies related to water leakage detection and 
localization, which are highly relevant to the work carried out in this 
paper. In addition, articles addressing the practical application of water 
leakage detection and localization methodologies and ML techniques 
were included to provide valuable insights into the current state of 
development in this research domain. To support this process, Sco-
pus (2019) was chosen as the primary search database, as it indexes 
high-quality and reputable journals and conference proceedings.
In addition to the scientific review, a commercial analysis was 
conducted on the available leak detection and localization technolo-
gies. However, unlike scientific research, commercial solutions are not 
systematically indexed in dedicated databases. Well-known scientific 
databases, such as Scopus or Web of Science, predominantly include 
peer-reviewed academic publications rather than commercial technolo-
gies, which are typically documented in public company documenta-
tion and technical reports. Consequently, the commercial analysis was 
conducted with this limitation in mind, incorporating keywords such 
as ‘‘water supply systems’’, ‘‘detection and localization’’, ‘‘leak monitor-
ing’’, and ‘‘commercial solutions’’. Furthermore, the eligible companies 
were required to (1) demonstrate global activity and operation within 
the sector, (2) have several years of operation (market experience), (3)

Lastly, for the industrial review, several databases are available 
for patent searches, including platforms provided by major patent 
offices such as the European Patent Office (EPO) through Espacenet 
(2023) and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) 
through Patent Public Search (USPTO, 2024). However, the results 
from these databases are subject to limitations arising from the vary-
ing criteria and classification systems established by their respec-
tive regulatory and evaluating entities. In contrast, Google Patents
(Google Patents, 2009) offers broader coverage, indexing documents 
from more than 100 major patent offices worldwide, including full-text 
patents from 20 of the largest offices. This makes it a strong rival to 
the EPO’s Espacenet in terms of comprehensiveness; therefore, it was 
chosen as the preferred platform and database for the industrial review.
The selection criteria for the industrial review were implemented 
in two phases. A global search query was formulated, incorporating 
keywords related to the water sector, including ‘‘water leakage’’ and 
‘‘water distribution systems’’, among others. This search query was 
then combined with two additional, more topic-oriented search queries. 
First, a search query comprising specific keywords, such as ‘‘machine 
learning’’ or ‘‘neural network’’, was employed to identify patents using 
software-based techniques. In the second phase, keywords such as 
‘‘acoustic sensor’’ or ‘‘thermal imaging camera’’ were used to identify 
hardware-based techniques. Building on these preliminary results, a 
rapid screening of the identified patents was conducted based on 
two criteria: (1) application status, whereby only patents marked as 
‘‘application granted’’1 and with the state ‘‘active’’ were included, and 
(2) the relevance of the title and abstract content in determining the 
suitability of the patent for water supply systems.
3. Scientific review: Water leakage detection and localization
It is known that some piping system conditions lead to periodic 
failure (Lopez et al., 2025), which can be prevented by adopting appro-
priate leakage management strategies, as schematically represented in 
Fig. 3. Before the network operation, hydraulic stability and robustness 
should be checked to ensure the pressure requirements, pipe’s reliabil-
ity, safety, and leak tightness (Zaman et al., 2020; Lopez et al., 2025; 
Abdulshaheed et al., 2017).
During the network operation, some measures include: preven-
tion, assessment, regulation, control, detection and localization, and 
repair (Wan et al., 2022; Zaman et al., 2020). Prevention and as-
sessment steps help to identify problematic pipes with non-destructive 
inspections (Hawari et al., 2020) and water audits to estimate the 
volume of water loss, searching for possible background leaks (Zaman 
et al., 2020; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Puust et al., 2010; Gupta and Kulat, 
2018; AL-Washali et al., 2020). The regulation and control stages 
include policy measures and KPIs’ analysis, as well as on-site visual 
inspection with consumer reports and/or pressure management tools 
combined with online optimization software (Zaman et al., 2020; Z. 
Hu et al., 2021). Nevertheless, according to Puust et al. (2010) and Da-
wood et al. (2020), these approaches are costly, labor-intensive, and 
time-consuming.
The detection and localization step is the most complex stage of the 
leakage management process, and where several different techniques 
and approaches can be used to detect and locate the leak (Wan et al., 
2022; Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020). Usually, the detection

perspective, leak detection and localization methodologies rely on the 
analysis of hydraulic and mechanical disturbances caused by leakage in 
pressurized networks. Depending on the methodology approach, these 
disturbances may be captured directly by sensing devices or inferred 
indirectly through hydraulic modeling and data analysis.
3.1. Hardware-based methods
As shown in Fig. 4, hardware-based methods are defined according 
to the used device and how it interacts with the pipe network. They 
can be distinguished between intrusive (‘‘in-pipe’’) and non-intrusive 
(‘‘out-pipe’’) devices, where according to Zaman et al. (2020) the main 
difference is whether they are temporarily inserted into a pipeline for 
periodic inspection and data collection or detect leaks by measuring 
pipe characteristics from the outside of the pipe.
Intrusive devices can be classified based on the type of commu-
nication and energy, autonomy, sensor, and motion strategy. This 
classification goes from tethered to battery-powered devices (Zaman 
et al., 2020); non-autonomous controlled by trained users to fully 
autonomous with real-time sensoring (Negm et al., 2023); passive 
or active motion approach, whether it relies on water flow or an 
actuator for motion, such as wheeled, track, legged, inchworm or 
snake type (Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020). In the context of 
intrusive devices, Kazeminasab et al. (2021) present an in-pipe robot 
designed for inspection in pressurized water pipes. This technology 
enables the inspection of the pipe in inaccessible parts of the network 
in a semi-autonomous way. However, it has some limitations, includ-
ing the reproducibility in other networks, due to the complexity and 
diversity of its design, the need for wireless communication, and the 
length limitation associated with tethered devices. Another example of 
a hardware device is the Pipeline Inspection Gauge (PIG) (Yue, 2024; 
Zhang et al., 2020), as illustrated in Fig. 5(a), useful for removing 
possible deposits in pipes, assessing pipe condition and detecting leak 
events (Negm et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the traditional PIG device is 
not the optimal choice for use in pipes with higher flows or narrower 
pipes, when compared with the ‘‘smart’’ PIG device, which has been 
demonstrated to offer superior performance in such contexts, such as 
the smartball from Xylem (2021b), WRc (2022), which is represented 
in Fig. 5(b).
Regarding non-intrusive devices, these detect leaks by measuring 
pipe characteristics such as flow and pressure or even acoustics from 
the outside of the pipe, as mentioned in Zaman et al. (2020), Niebuhr 
et al. (2019). These include acoustic devices that rely on leakage-
induced vibrations or noise signals to detect leaks with microphones, 
geophones, accelerometers, and/or correlators, among others as pre-
sented in Negm et al. (2023), El-Zahab and Zayed (2019), Zaman 
et al. (2020). Other examples include infrared thermography, remote 
sensing, radiography, EM scanning and ultrasonic methods (Wan et al., 
2022; Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020). Relatively a non-intrusive 
technique, such as ground penetrating radar (GPR), the work of Wang 
et al. (2025) proposes a full-polarimetric GPR to assess and identify 
pipe structural changes which may be indicative of leaks. In comparison 
with traditional GPR, the proposed FP-GPR do not require complex 
data processing, expert interpretation, allowing a more standardized 
and automated interpretation analysis. Furthermore, the integration

Notwithstanding the previous literature, acoustic sensors and tech-
niques are the most widely used to detect water leaks and measure 
data. The majority of authors combine acoustic data measurements 
with software analysis techniques to achieve a greater result. The 
hydrophone is one of the most frequently used devices to collect data,

method, while Sohn et al. (2025) implements a multifractal analysis 
of the acoustic signals. Although this technology is highly efficient in 
terms of the detection process, it can be both time-consuming and costly

in larger water networks (Bakhtawar and Zayed, 2021). Correlation-

Additionally, some authors employ ML models to analyze this acous-
tic data, proposing hybrid approaches. CNN models have been em-
ployed by several authors, presenting multiple time series-based ap-
proaches (Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2021). Ma 
et al. (2025) uses a temporal segmentation-based approach to analyze 
the acoustic signal combined with a CNN to recognize Mel spectro-
gram features, while Zhang et al. (2023) proposes a pseudo-siamese 
CNN model that integrates Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients and 
time–frequency domain features extracted from acoustic signals. More-
over, Guo et al. (2021) use a time–frequency CNN to analyze acoustic 
signals and identify leak signals. The model performance is compared 
with other ML models. Furthermore, other studies have employed the 
Random Forest (RF) model as a classifier in place of the CNN model, 
as evidenced by the research conducted by Cheng and Shen (2022) 
and Guo et al. (2020).
Achieving favorable outcomes with acoustic sensors requires a high 
density of sensor strategic placement throughout the network, which is 
costly and uncommon, particularly in large-scale real WSS (Chew et al., 
2023). Fig. 6 illustrates the influence of the leakage situation acoustic 
waves on the sensors. Further details about non-intrusive techniques 
can be found in Müller et al. (2021), Ballantine et al. (1997), Awwad 
et al. (2020), Bimpas et al. (2011), Petrov et al. (2023), Niebuhr et al. 
(2019), Chen et al. (2024).
As a result, intrusive and non-intrusive approaches provide high 
accuracy according to Wan et al. (2022) and Zaman et al. (2020), 
however, intrusive devices are less time-consuming and more cost-
effective, and non-intrusive are more time-consuming, costly, and 
labor-intensive, requiring professional staff. Additionally, hardware-
based leak detection approaches are difficult to use without suspending 
regular service, and can only be temporary, requiring partial removal 
after inspection (Zaman et al., 2020). It is also affected by external fac-
tors, such as ambient temperature, soil characteristics, and seasonality, 
among others (Zaman et al., 2020).
Overall, these findings indicate that the effectiveness of hardware-
based approaches is strongly context-dependent. Intrusive devices may 
offer faster and more cost-effective detection in controlled environ-
ments, however, their application is constrained by operational in-
terruptions and accessibility limitations. Non-intrusive techniques, al-
though less disruptive to service, often require extensive network sen-
sorization and remain highly sensitive to environmental and soil condi-
tions. Consequently, hardware-based methods tend to be more suitable 
for targeted inspections or high-priority areas rather than continuous 
large-scale monitoring in complex urban networks. These constraints 
increase the interest in combining hardware-based sensing devices 
with advanced data processing and software-based methods to enhance 
accuracy, robustness and scalability in leak detection strategies (see 
Table 1).
3.2. Software-based methods
Software-based methods rely on the calculation and analysis of data 
using hydraulic models to obtain information regarding leakage, which 
can be employed for continuous leak detection (Negm et al., 2023). 
These data are essential to undergo a processing phase to ensure the 
accuracy and reliability of the results. According to Wan et al. (2022), 
the process is divided into five main steps: goal identification, data 
collection, data preparation, data analysis methods and performance 
evaluation. The initial steps enable the definition of the needs and 
objectives, aligned with data collection characteristics from synthetic 
datasets and/or historical monitoring data with real leakage events. 
Data preparation and pre-processing are required to remove aspects 
such as embedded data noise, missing data, and/or data from defective 
recorders, which influence the detection accuracy (Wu and Liu, 2017). 
Additionally, leak detection techniques need to be chosen to analyze 
the data, and finally, previously defined KPIs validate the model’s 
performance.

3.2.1. Model-based approaches
Model-based techniques (see Fig. 7) require accurate and well-
calibrated models in order to compare the simulation observable vari-
ables, such as pressure and flow, predicted by the hydraulic model 
with the real measurements. This monitoring task allows the continuous 
detection of potential leaks (Wan et al., 2022; Negm et al., 2023; Barros 
et al., 2024; Rajabi et al., 2023).
According to Zaman et al. (2020), the model-based detection ap-
proach requires building a hydraulic model, which needs to be cal-
ibrated and validated before applying leak detection strategies. This 
model is based on real operation conditions simulated on an ex-
tended period simulation (EPS) using hydraulic simulators such as 
EPANET (Rossman, 2000), WNTR (Klise et al., 2017), OpenFlows 
Water (Lesli, 2024), among others (Negm et al., 2023; Z. Hu et al., 
2021; Zaman et al., 2020). Therefore, a calibrated hydraulic model 
will accurately represent the water system, which can be used as 
a digital twin with fewer errors (Wan et al., 2022; Zaman et al., 
2020). Nevertheless, this well-calibrated hydraulic model requires a 
substantial volume of data, and time investment, since it is not a 
universal feature amongst all water utilities (Chu et al., 2025; Nimri 
et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 2017).
Concerning leak detection strategies, Zaman et al. (2020) catego-
rized them as direct or indirect methods, whether it is a simple pressure 
comparison or a more complex mathematical operation relying on a 
hydraulic model. The most common direct method is the pressure resid-
ual vector (PRV), which compares the theoretical simulated pressure 
for non-leak scenarios with different leak scenarios for a predefined 
threshold (Wan et al., 2022; Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020). The

Sensitivity analysis-based methods (Fig. 8(b)) compare simulated

and pressure residuals for leak and non-leak scenarios, helping corre-

example of the application of the sensitivity-based method is the work 
of Wu et al. (2025), which uses this method to calibrate the roughness 
coefficient and effectively locate leakage. The result of this process is 
a pressure-roughness sensitivity matrix, which simultaneously seeks to 
improve the robustness of sensor placement in larger water networks. 
Additionally, this type of method can also be applied to examine the 
pipe material influence in the pressure residual matrix to improve 
the accuracy and reduce external factors uncertainty, as can be seen 
in Abdulshaheed et al. (2018).
Finally, the classification-based approach (Fig. 8(c)) is a statistical 
method that uses a classifier automatically trained using ML techniques 
as described by Wan et al. (2022). This classifier creates a pressure 
residual map of the different leak scenarios, which enables training the 
model to determine the possible leakage area when a leak is detected. 
This methodology is applied by Mohammed et al. (2021), where a 
binary classifier is trained with data given by a calibrated hydraulic 
model of pressure and flow. The performance of the proposed methods 
is assessed by comparing the classification results with those obtained 
using the minimum night flow approach in the literature.
According to Wan et al. (2022), the main advantage of calibration 
methods is to determine the leak location and water volume. However, 
they usually require high computational resources for a large number of 
decision variables, which is the reason for them being mainly applied to 
smaller networks (Wan et al., 2022; Sophocleous et al., 2019; Berglund 
et al., 2017). Regarding the sensitivity analysis approach, one of the 
disadvantages is the residual constraint, since theoretically, for a non-
leakage scenario this value is zero, but in practice, measurements and 
calibration errors, and external noise affect model performance (Wan 
et al., 2022; Nimri et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 2017). Finally, the main 
advantage of the classification approaches is the ability to produce a 
large amount of training data, however it requires a well-calibrated 
hydraulic model, which is complex task as explained by Wan et al. 
(2022).
Therefore, model-based methods depend on the hydraulic model pa-
rameters, which always have uncertainties. They are affected by factors 
such as (1) measurement errors in pressure and flow sensors (Wan et al., 
2022; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Moser et al., 2017; Wu and Liu, 2017), (2) 
nodal demands, which are challenging to measure (Blesa and Pérez, 
2018), (3) unknown pipe conditions, since the ageing process increases 
the roughness coefficient and decreases the pipe diameters (Adedeji 
et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2018; Wu and Liu, 2017), and (4) simplifi-
cations made during the hydraulic modeling process, which can lead 
to unrealistic system representations (Wan et al., 2022). Furthermore, 
it has been demonstrated that model-based methods will yield more 
favorable results when measurement sensors are optimally placed and 
well as high-resolution measurements (Chu et al., 2025; Nimri et al., 
2023; Oberascher et al., 2024).
In conclusion, although model-based approaches benefit from strong 
physical interpretability and consistency with hydraulic principles, 
their performance is highly conditioned by data reliability and net-
work complexity. These methods tend to achieve more robust re-
sults in well-instrumented systems with stable demand patterns and 
accurate hydraulic models, however, in large-scale networks with 
sparse monitoring, high demand uncertainty, or poorly characterized 
infrastructure, their performance may deteriorate.
3.2.2. Data-driven approaches
Data-driven techniques, compared to model-based, do not require a 
complete understanding of the hydraulic system and equations. How-
ever, these often rely on large quantities and quality of historical data to 
typically perform well (Negm et al., 2023; Barros et al., 2024; Rajabi 
et al., 2023; Chu et al., 2025). In real-world systems, data is mostly 
collected using sensors, including pressure, flow, and demands, with 
different sampling time intervals (Zaman et al., 2020). Due to this, data 
must be carefully analyzed and pre-processed. This step may be very 
time-consuming, as it aims to clean and organize the collected data, and 
includes tasks as data sorting, filtering, and transforming, while taking 
into account sensor and reading uncertainties, incorrect data, missing 
samples, and even unlabeled data (Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 
2020; Wu et al., 2024a; Wu and Liu, 2017). However, it is important 
to note that in some circumstances, even with the pre-processing, the 
information may not be sensitive to small leak flow rates (Negm et al., 
2023). Many recent data-driven approaches rely on ML algorithms to 
analyze large volumes of sensor data and detect anomalous behavior 
associated with leaks.
For leak detection, data-driven methods can be classified based on 
type, data source, and technique, and can be distinguished between 
supervised and unsupervised approaches. Supervised methods require a 
labeled dataset, where leak and non-leak samples are clearly identified 
and provided, while unsupervised approaches do not, and focus on 
statistical or clustering analysis to identify different data groups (Zaman 
et al., 2020; Quiñones-Grueiro et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2024a). As for 
data-source, methods can be regarded as flow-based, pressure-based, 
demand-based, flow & pressure-based or demand & pressure-based 
(although demands are measured as flows) (Zaman et al., 2020).
Data-driven techniques require data analysis and mathematical cal-
culations including classification, prediction-classification, statistical, 
clustering and signal processing, as mentioned in Wan et al. (2022), 
Negm et al. (2023), Z. Hu et al. (2021), Zaman et al. (2020), Wu et al. 
(2024a). Nonetheless, independent of the approach or method, all of 
them rely on the abundance of available observed data, as previously 
mentioned (Negm et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2020), as well as labeled 
data for specific methods (Nimri et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 2017). 
Classification methods distinguish normal from outlier data using a 
classification model, which has both states as input (Negm et al., 
2023; Zaman et al., 2020; Mohan Doss et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 
2017). The training process with labeled data is essential to ensure 
the model’s performance and accuracy, typically yielding a binary 
output (Nimri et al., 2023; Mohan Doss et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 
2017). The predominant approach involves the use of an ML model 
as a binary classifier model, with multiple literature works combining 
acoustic sensor information with ML classification. For instance, Guo 
et al. (2021) use a time–frequency CNN, while Peng et al. (2024) 
applies a logarithmic spectrogram combined with a ResNet CNN model, 
comparing their performance with other ML models. Other types of 
input are also leveraged, with Shah and Patel (2024) using demands, 
pressure and residual chlorine values for a NN.
Alternatively, prediction-classification methods only require normal 
data for the training process (Wu and Liu, 2017). Initially, a predictive 
model is trained to predict the normal system behavior, then a clas-
sification process is carried out to compare and evaluate the real and 
predicted outcomes (Wan et al., 2022; Negm et al., 2023; Z. Hu et al., 
2021; Zaman et al., 2020; Wu and Liu, 2017). Prediction-classification 
methods are also commonly used throughout the literature (Glynis 
et al., 2023; McMillan et al., 2023; Wan et al., 2023a; Örn Garðarsson 
et al., 2022). All these works use flow and/or pressure predictions 
to calculate the residual matrix when compared with the historical 
and real-time data. Subsequently, these values assess the probability of 
exceeding a pre-defined threshold and represent a leak situation. Addi-
tionally, Cody et al. (2020) replace numerical flow and pressure data 
acoustic signals instead, combining them with linear prediction analysis 
to observe the pipe-fluid response. Finally, Rajabi et al. (2023) adopts

Statistical methods do not include any advanced prediction or clas-
sification stage, only relying on statistical theory. Among these, SPC is 
the most popular approach, leveraging control charts to monitor mea-
surement variation (Negm et al., 2023; Wu and Liu, 2017). However, 
statistical approaches assume that data follows a standard Gaussian 
distribution and that errors are uncorrelated over time, which limits 
their application and may have high uncertainty (Wan et al., 2022; Wu 
and Liu, 2017). For instance, Cai et al. (2023) employs simpler statis-
tical methods, such as the X-bar and cumulative sum control chart, to 
detect leaks. In contrast, Xie et al. (2024) and Wan et al. (2023b) adopt 
more complex approaches. The first authors use Bayesian inference to 
estimate the leakage probability on a leak assumption hydraulic model, 
while the second authors apply a methodology that does not require 
a hydraulic model, based on a statistic-based EWMA-enhanced Tukey 
technique, incorporating a moving time-window.
Clustering approaches are unsupervised methods which compare 
the time series with reference values without adjusting the prediction 
model (Wan et al., 2022; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020). 
Such techniques result in reduced uncertainties when compared with 
prediction-classification approaches and can be formulated taking into 
account data from hydraulic models or not (Nimri et al., 2023; Mohan 
Doss et al., 2023). Regarding some practical application studies, Min 
et al. (2022) applies the K-means clustering algorithm, one of the 
simplest approaches, to detect leakage data. While Cimorelli et al. 
(2025) deploys a minimization process between real and predicted 
values, whilst implementing a filtering-clustering algorithm to reduce 
the nodes with minimal probability of representing a leak point. More-
over, Han et al. (2024) and X. Hu et al. (2021) propose the same 
density-based spatial clustering approach with noise. This methodology 
subdivided the network into smaller regions to be evaluated. When 
compared with more traditional methods such as SVM and KNN, the 
framework obtained better results.
Finally, digital signal processing methods use pressure and/or acous-
tic signals to identify leak patterns, including approaches such as 
pressure point analysis (PPA), whereby pressure measurements are 
statistically analyzed over time. Aligned with this, Barros et al. (2024) 
employ an ICA method to differentiate between leak patterns and 
normal behavior, while Harmouche and Narasimhan (2020) apply 
association rule mining to analyze this information. Furthermore, Luo 
et al. (2025) uses time and frequency data to disaggregate these 
signals into trend and residual components, thereby refining the leak 
detection process. A schematic representation of some of the previously 
mentioned methods is shown in Fig. 9.
Overall, compared to model-based techniques, data-driven methods 
may be easier to implement, as they do not require in-depth knowledge 
of the hydraulic system, as well as specific information on the net-
work’s physical characteristics. However, they often require substantial 
volumes of data to perform accordingly, which presents a significant 
limitation for real-world implementation. As for methodologies, data-
driven methods offer a wide variety of possible approaches, each suited 
to specific situations. Classification methods are useful for scenarios 
where leak information is available and identified, a condition that may 
not happen in real scenarios. This limitation makes purely classification 
methods unfeasible in such cases (Wu and Liu, 2017). Conversely, 
clustering or signal processing methods are suitable for situations where

3.2.3. Hybrid approaches
There are alternative approaches that integrate different detection 
techniques or knowledge-based methods, which rely on sophisticated 
computational formulations and domain-specific knowledge. Examples 
include ANNs, fuzzy logic, and artificial intelligence (AI) (Negm et al., 
2023; Zaman et al., 2020), in which the implementation of ML models 
facilitates automated data analysis. These hybrid approaches enhance 
the efficiency of the detection and localization process by using the 
most effective aspects of each method to achieve a superior solu-
tion. For instance, a hybrid method can combine the knowledge of 
pressure residuals used in model-based approaches with a classifier 
as a data-driven approach (Zaman et al., 2020), thus gaining the 
advantages of both techniques. Nevertheless, it should be noted that 
the combination of these techniques is also subject to inherent limi-
tations and disadvantages. For instance, the use of a well-calibrated 
hydraulic model in model-based approaches and a large quantity of 
high-quality data in data-driven methods are limiting conditions (Chu 
et al., 2025). In algorithms with detection and localization modules, the 
data-driven approach is typically used for the detection module, while 
the model-based approach is used for the localization module.
Corzo et al. (2023) proposed a methodology that combines a data-
driven model and clustering to detect and localize leaks. The authors 
employed a calibrated hydraulic model to generate a dataset and 
calculate the residual vectors. These vectors are then clustered to 
select the most representative nodes. Subsequently, the pressure val-
ues in a leak and non-leak scenario are compared to locate multiple 
leaks. Oberascher et al. (2025) implemented a graph-based GA that es-
tablishes a topological relationship between the leak candidates’ nodes 
and sizes. This approach yielded superior outcomes when compared to 
traditional GA and MILP algorithms. Furthermore, Chew et al. (2023) 
presented a series of studies by different authors that employed deep 
learning algorithms to process acoustic sensor signals for detection 
and localization. In addition, physics-informed models demonstrate 
enhanced potential due to their capacity to use physical principles to 
incorporate more information in the ML model, thereby helping to 
predict pressure and flow, as shown in Ye et al. (2022), Ashraf et al. 
(2024).
In general, hybrid techniques represent a structured attempt to 
overcome the intrinsic limitations presented by the other leak detection 
approaches. The integration of hydraulic modeling with the adapt-
ability of data-driven models and, even with direct hardware sensing 
technologies is a key aspect of hybrid methodologies. These aim to 
enhance robustness and accuracy under uncertain operational condi-
tions. Notwithstanding, this integration increases system complexity, 
requires careful synchronization between modeling and data-processing 
modules, and often demands higher computational and infrastructural 
resources. Therefore, hybrid approaches offer a promising scalable 
and resilient leak detection, their practical applications are dependent

A comprehensive review from the different methodologies reveals 
a structural trade-off between physical interpretability, computational 
scalability, and data dependency, when considered hardware-based and 
software-based (model-based and data-driven) approaches. Despite the 
fact that hardware-based methods provide a direct physical inspection 
and higher precision localization, they are limited in terms of scalability 
and operational cost. Conversely, software-based approaches rely on 
hydraulic modeling fidelity (in the case of model-based) and/or data 
representative availability (in the case of data-driven), introducing 
uncertainty and transferability challenges. It is evident that the applica-
tion of hybrid methods, integrating diverse methodologies, enable the 
extension of their application across different scenarios and justifies the 
growing interest in these methodologies.
3.2.4. Machine learning techniques applied to water supply systems
As previously mentioned, ML represents a powerful application 
within the domain of AI and WSS, whereby algorithms and models are 
developed to enable tasks to be performed without the need for explicit 
instructions (Géron, 2019). As the complexity of the WSS increases, ML 
models can help to dynamically process vast quantities of information, 
allowing the identification of relationships within the data and the 
acquisition of knowledge from previous experiences. This automatic 
process increases the efficiency of this time-consuming task, becom-
ing a feasible and economical alternative to other more traditional 
approaches (Nakhaei et al., 2022; Rapp et al., 2023; Lunani, 2018; 
Doorn, 2021; Garzón et al., 2022; Basnet et al., 2023; Negm et al., 2024; 
Wu et al., 2024b; Nimri et al., 2023). Furthermore, the integration of 
ML models with digital system representations (digital twins) facilitates 
the development of more analytical capabilities and functionalities as 
described in Pereira et al. (2025).
Although ML methods are generally considered part of data-driven 
approaches (Mota et al., 2025), they are discussed separately in this 
review. These techniques are increasingly used across different leakage 
detection frameworks, being applied in purely data-driven scenarios 
as well as integrated with hydraulic models in model-based or hybrid 
approaches. Currently, these models are used in various aspects of WSS, 
including leak detection and localization, fault prediction, anomaly 
and attack detection in sensors, hydraulic state estimation prediction, 
water consumption forecast, direct control optimization, data handling 
calibration, network design, and others (Pereira et al., 2025; Wu et al., 
2024a; Wang et al., 2025a). The most popular subjects of application 
are leak detection and localization, where ML models help with the 
analysis of historical datasets to identify leak patterns and establish 
relationships between them; fault prediction, which is beneficial in min-
imizing pipe breaks and potential future leaks; and hydraulic estimation 
that enables the prediction of the subsequent hydraulic state that 
reproduces the real operation (Pereira et al., 2025; Rapp et al., 2023). 
In the context of water leak detection and localization in WSS, Table 3 
presents a summary of framework approaches and main limitations of 
ML of some recent works.
In the field of fault prediction, Beig Zali et al. (2025) proposed a 
combination of multiple ML classification algorithms to predict pipe 
failure using historical data, focused on binary classification. Despite 
the approach achieving good performance results, it strongly relies on 
historical failure data availability. Moreover, it disregards environmen-
tal factors, e.g. weather data, soil conditions, or pipe material, which 
can impact failure rates.
Regarding the analysis of acoustic sensor signals in a WSS, Fares 
et al. (2023) conducted a parametric study of multiple ML techniques, 
including Decision Tree (DT), RF, ANNs, DL, among others. The study 
compared these models across different datasets. When analyzing the 
F1-score and AUC metrics of the models’ performance, it was es-
tablished that the ensemble tree-based methods achieved the highest 
performance on the known datasets. In contrast, DL and ANN demon-
strated greater stability when applied to unknown data, with the ability 
to correctly identify 10 out of 11 leak situations. Nevertheless, chal-
lenges such as background noise variability, limited generalization, 
and the potential requirement for manual signal pre-processing persist, 
thereby constraining transferability to other networks.
Furthermore, several studies also apply CNN-based models to an-
alyze acoustic signals (Boadu et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2024; Xu 
et al., 2025). Boadu et al. (2025) combined a CNN with conventional 
classifiers to create an ensemble model that uses the complementary 
strengths of all algorithms. This has been demonstrated to achieve 
higher favorable results. Nevertheless, the results remain highly de-
pendent on data quality and manual feature selection, which limit the 
applicability in other systems. A more complex approach was tested 
by Peng et al. (2024). The study involved the comparison of denoised 
logarithmic spectrograms combined with a CNN model based on ResNet 
structure with more classical ML approaches. This complex approach 
requires representative consumption patterns in addition to manual 
pre-processing, potentially reducing generalization across different net-
works. Finally, Xu et al. (2025) demonstrated that signal transformation 
combined with a CNN classifier can improve model performance and 
accuracy without requiring hydraulic modeling information.
Additionally, Tang et al. (2025) presented a Multi-View Embed-
ding Distance Feature Fusion Network (MDFF), which integrates time-, 
frequency-, and wavelet-domain features of a pipeline vibration signal. 
This methodology offers enhanced accuracy in comparison with single-
view models. However, the validation process has been restricted to 
experimental networks, raising concerns about its applicability and per-
formance in water networks with lower density and reliability sensors.
In contrast to acoustic signal approaches, McMillan et al. (2024) 
propose a domain-informed Variational Autoencoder (VAE) combined 
with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier to detect leaks us-
ing water flow time series data with high accuracy. Nonetheless, the 
methodology is predicated on the assumption that historical leak-
free consumption patterns remain representative over time, that high-
quality training data is available, and that previous knowledge of the 
system is known. Momeni et al. (2022) explored a hybrid approach, 
using an ANN model as a predictive tool for hydraulic simulation, and 
combining it with evolutionary optimization algorithms to effectively 
localize leaks based on emitter coefficients. This approach has been 
proven to be effective in controlled conditions, however, it requires 
real-time data availability and accurate network parameters, which 
might not be a common reality in real-world systems.
Overall, it can be seen that authors mostly focus on two main 
types of input data to mostly conduct leak detection and localization. 
Some authors leverage acoustic or vibration signals, focused on the 
physical and local manifestation of leaks, with these methods mostly 
requiring a feature engineering step of time- and frequency-domain fea-
ture extraction. Others focus on hydraulic time-series analysis, relying 
system-level responses, and use data such as pressure or flow pattern 
deviations and anomalies. Although different, both methodologies re-
quire high data quality and quantity to perform well (Chen et al., 2025; 
Jakubik et al., 2024). This is one of their biggest limitations, especially 
considering real-world implementations, where sensors and data acqui-
sition devices for leak detection may be expensive, with water utilities 
not recognizing its cost–benefit trade-off (Chen et al., 2025). Another 
significant trend is the use of Deep Learning models for leak detection, 
with several authors exploring such approaches (Boadu et al., 2025; 
Peng et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; McMillan et al., 
2024; Momeni et al., 2022). However, DL models usually lead to very 
high computational costs, possibly hindering their application in real-
time scenarios. Nonetheless, such methods have proven to be better 
performing than more common, simpler ML approaches.

3.2.5. Leak detection and localization performance parameters
Following the established by IWA in ‘‘Standard Definition of Wa-
ter Losses’’ (Pearson, 2019), Performance Indicators (PI) facilitate a 
comparative analysis of performance metrics across different water 
utilities. PI can be analyzed for Non-Revenue Water (NRW), Apparent 
Losses (AL), and Real Losses (RL). The recommended PI for Real Losses 
is established and referred to as the infrastructure leakage analysis 
(ILI), which is the ratio of the current (CARL) and the unavoidable 
(UARL) annual volume of real losses. This enables an assessment of the 
efficacy of the distribution network in terms of maintenance, repair and 
rehabilitation.
In addition, other Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) can be used 
to evaluate and assess the software-based models’ performance itself in 
a measurable and quantifiable way. Therefore, to analyze the models’ 
performance for the detection process, the Mean Absolute Percentage 
Error (MAPE), True Positive Rate (TPR), False Positive Rate (FPR), 
Detection Accuracy (DA), and Detection Time (DT) are mostly em-
ployed (Wan et al., 2022; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020). Table 4 
summarizes the main model KPIs for the detection process, where 𝑋𝑖 is 
the measured value, ̂𝑋𝑖 is the predicted value, and 𝑁 is the number of 
samples. Also, TP defines the True Positives (burst correctly detected), 
FN the False Negatives (burst not detected), FP the False Positives (the 
burst did not occur but was misdetected), and TN the True Negatives 
(no burst and no detection) (Wang et al., 2020; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Wan 
et al., 2022). Detection time (DT) is the time from the start of the burst 
to the alarm, which is directly proportional to the leak damage. A good 
detection method should have high TPR and DA and low MAPE, FPR
and DT values (Wan et al., 2022; Z. Hu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020). 
Detection methods can also be classified through qualitative KPIs, as 
demonstrated by Farah and Shahrour (2024).
The localization process is subjected to a more qualitative analy-
sis, where the KPIs provide intuitive insights into the leak location. 
Moreover, there is no consensus among the various authors regarding 
the optimal localization KPIs (Wan et al., 2022). According to Wan 
et al. (2022), this can be measured as the geographical distance to 
the leak, the pipe distance to the leak, or the classification accuracy. 
On the other hand, Z. Hu et al. (2021) used the Average Topological 
Distance (ATD), which is the average of the smallest distance between 
the leaking node and the selected possible nodes. Table 6 provides a 
comparative analysis of the various KPIs employed by different authors 
in the field.
Despite acknowledging the substantial influence of system and 
methodology on the outcomes of KPIs, and the consequent impossibility 
of direct comparison between results obtained in benchmark and real 
systems, it is evident that data-driven methods are the most prevalent 
for water leakage detection, with a particular emphasis on prediction-
classification and clustering-based approaches. This is largely used 
because the detection process is typically binary, distinguishing be-
tween leaks and non-leaks, and using a significant amount of sensor 
data information allows for its development and general use. The met-
rics mentioned above, including TPR, FPR, FP, and DT, are frequently 
used in these methods.
It can be further concluded that, even for different real case studies, 
the lowest rate for well-identified losses (TPR) is 71.4% (Wu et al.,

the percentage is less than 10% for all the case studies presented. 
Finally, the cases that considered the DT (Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 
2020), reached a total time of less than 10 minutes to detect the leak.

3.2.6. Practical application and benchmarking: the case of BattLeDIM
To evaluate the efficacy of the detection and localization meth-
ods previously outlined without compromising the functionality of 
WSS, benchmarking case studies can be employed. These case studies 
are typically based on theoretical real-case scenarios, yet they are 
meticulously designed to contain all the essential information required 
for effective analysis and testing. An example of a benchmark for 
leakage studies is BattLeDIM (Battle of Leakage Detection and Iso-
lation Methods), a network that was presented in an international 
competition organized as part of the 2nd International CCWI/WDSA 
Joint Conference 2020 (Vrachimis et al., 2022). This benchmark was 
proposed by Vrachimis et al. (2022), and it is based on L-Town, a small 
hypothetical town in a city in Cyprus, as represented in Fig. 11. This 
complex network has 782 junctions, 905 pipes, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank, 1 
pump, 3 relief valves, and 33 pressure sensors to monitor the system.
A total of 18 teams from different countries participated in the com-
petition. The information given to each participant was: (1) network 
model, (2) nominal model, and (3) historical datasets. The network 
model provided was a virtual network, used to generate the data. In 
contrast, the nominal model, which differs from the real one, was 
presented in the form of an EPANET hydraulic simulation file format 
containing the network information. The historical SCADA datasets 
provided information from 2018 and 2019 of pressure sensors, con-
sumption demands from DMA C, flows from reservoirs, and pump and 
tank levels. Additionally, it was given a file comprising the previous 
abrupt and gradual leaks identified and rectified in 2018. The total 
number of leaks presented was 33 (14 in 2018, where 4 were not de-
tected, and 19 in 2019). Finally, the contestants’ solution was evaluated 
using an economics approach, considering the water saved and repair 
costs, as well as critical parameters such as detection time (less than 
one week) and maximum distance (300 m).
The top teams’ solutions are based on hybrid approaches, which 
combine data-driven techniques based on observed real data to detect 
possible leaks with model-based approaches that use hydraulic models 
to localize the leak (BattLeDIM, 2020).
The Tongji team’s proposal, from Li and Xin (2020), Li et al. 
(2022), included a Multiple Leak Detection and Localization Frame-
work (MLDLF), whose methodology approach is illustrated in Fig. 
12. The MLDLF framework integrates an EPANET simulation module, 
which is used to generate data measurements to be used in calibration, 
identification and localization steps. To calibrate the hydraulic model 
in terms of pipe roughness and node demands, a gradient-based algo-
rithm and a pressure sensitivity matrix are used. After calibration, the 
identification step uses a Seasonal-Trend Decomposition using Loess 
(STL) to analyze the pressure residual and cluster using K-means to 
classify leaks. Finally, the localization module used a ‘‘stepwise leakage 
localization’’ approach that creates a benchmark leakage dataset (by 
simulating leaks in each pipe), reducing the search area (based on 
similarity) and pinpoint the leak.
The Under Pressure team (Steffelbauer et al., 2020, 2022) developed 
a Dual Approach (DA) model, as represented in Fig. 13. The method-
ology proposed follows a hierarchical two-stage process: (1) demands 
and roughness calibration using time series analysis with EPANET data, 
(2) dual model for leak detection and localization. The dual model 
uses ‘‘real’’ pressure measurements at sensor nodes that are converted 
into virtual leak flows via virtual reservoirs, thereby transforming 
small pressure deviations into amplified leak signals. Therefore, the 
leak detection process is performed by analyzing flow residuals and 
applying change point detection methodologies, including Cumulative 
Sum (CUSUM), and likelihood-ratio tests. Regarding leak localization, 
pressure residuals and sensitivities matrix are considered to identify 
potential leak pipe candidates using the Pearson correlation.
The IRI team (Romero et al., 2020; Romero-Ben et al., 2022) ap-
plied two distinct methodologies depending on the density of pressure 
sensors, as depicted in Fig. 14. For situations with a high density 
of pressure sensors, a data-driven approach (see Fig. 14(a)) was em-
ployed to create two distinct network state models. These models were 
designed using the current data and historical non-leak conditions, 
employing graph-based interpolation with the network topology. This 
approach enables the approximation of the hydraulic state and the 
selection of leak pipe candidates. In opposite situations, with a low 
density of pressure sensor, a model-based approach (see Fig. 14(b)) is 
used. This approach requires a calibrated hydraulic model to simulate 
different leak scenarios and compare them with the real case scenario 
to determine the most likely leak location.
Leakbuster, led by Daniel et al. (2020, 2022), proposed a Leakage 
Identification and Localization Algorithm (LILA) comprising distinct de-
tection and localization models, as illustrated in Fig. 15. The detection 
model is a data-driven model that analyzes pressure data from sensors 
to distinguish between leaks and non-leaks. The leakage identification 
step uses a linear regression model, trained with non-leak data, to

to their underlying technological principles. These commercial imple-

in the scientific review, thereby illustrating the application of aca-
demic research into operational practice. In practice, the majority of 
commercialized systems rely on hardware-based sensing technologies, 
which remain the dominant approach in both residential applications 
and large-scale water distribution systems. Nevertheless, the degree 
of technological integration, scalability, and analytical sophistication 
varies considerably depending on the target application.

(2013), have implemented acoustic sensors, e.g., microphones and 
hydrophones, in combination with noise correlator systems capable of 
monitoring extensive pipeline sections. Table 7 summarizes the main 
commercial companies presented and their technological focus.
Beyond purely acoustic methods, additional hardware-based solu-
tions have been applied, including pressure and flow sensors integrated 
within smart metering infrastructures. These systems enable the iden-
tification of discrepancies at the District Metering Area (DMA) level 
through continuous monitoring and analysis of variations in hydraulic 
variables. While such sensor-based approaches have been shown to im-
prove scalability and support early warning mechanisms, they typically 
offer lower pinpoint localization accuracy compared to direct acoustic 
inspection. Their effectiveness depends on sensor density, data quality, 
and network configuration. Some examples of companies that have also 
applied this type of technology are WINT Water Intelligence (2020c), 
SUEZ worldwide (2022a), Veolia (2025a), Ovarro (2024c), SebaKMT 
(2013), HWM-Global (2016), Badger-Meter (2024a), TaKaDu (2011).
These companies report a substantial number of successful case 
studies in which their methodologies have been implemented. For 
instance, Gutermann (2012) reported case studies in which acoustic 
sensor monitoring enabled the identification of a substantial number 
of leaks over extensive network lengths, thus confirming its suitability 
for wide-area deployment. For example, in City of Logan (Gutermann, 
2021), 154 water leaks were repaired along the 2293 km water system 
within a 2-year period, while a Canadian pilot (Gutermann, 2020) 
identified 95 potential leaks over 180 km of inspected pipeline.
Moving to software-based approaches, the incorporation of analytics 
and AI has led to significant advancements in detection robustness. 
These data-driven platforms process acoustic signals, pressure measure-
ments, and consumption data using statistical methods, ML algorithms, 
and/or pattern recognition techniques. The objective of these systems 
is to minimize false alarms, automate interpretation, and enable remote 
monitoring. In this field, several companies (WINT Water Intelligence, 
2020c; FIDO Tech, 2021; AQS - Aquarius Spectrum, 2004a; Xylem, 
2021b; Veolia, 2025a; Echologics-Muller, 2016; Badger-Meter, 2024a; 
Itron, 2018; TaKaDu, 2011; SebaKMT, 2013; Ovarro, 2024c; HWM-
Global, 2016) apply AI-based methods to facilitate the transformation 
of raw sensor data into actionable signals through the implementa-
tion of signal classification, anomaly detection, and telemetry analysis. 
Despite the substantial improvement in automation and scalability, as 
already mentioned in the scientific review, their performance remains 
dependent on historical datasets, calibration procedures, and the repre-
sentativeness of training data, particularly when transferring solutions 
between different utilities.
Moreover, TaKaDu (2011) presents a list of successful case studies 
where their data-driven management platform, centered on system-
wide analytics rather than individual leak detection and localiza-
tion, has been implemented. In Queensland, Australia (TaKaDu, 2016, 
2021c, 2022b), TaKaDu’s interventions achieved savings of e14 million 
caused by underground leaks, which corresponded to 6.5 billion liters 
of water saved at the end of one year. The reactive response time to a 
leak was enhanced by 60%, and the repair time was reduced from 11 
days to less than 2 days. Also in the North Sydney, Australia (TaKaDu, 
2021b) case study, across more than 10 000 km of water network, a 
decrease of 34% of water loss was achieved in 2019–2020 compared 
to the 2015–2016 period.
To better balance the respective strengths and limitations of purely 
hardware- or purely software-based methods, an increasing number of 
companies have been implementing hybrid solutions that integrate tra-
ditional devices with software-based methodologies and AI to process 
sensor data. This change is indicative of an industry-wide trend that 
aims to improve scalability, reduce response times, and enable network-
wide monitoring rather than localized inspections. Hybrid solutions 
have emerged as a response to the limitations of purely hardware- or 
purely software-based approaches, improving detection sensitivity and 
the maintenance of localization reliability, especially for large water 
networks with high levels of monitoring and sensorization.
Satellite-based technologies have appeared as an alternative, with 
companies such as SUEZ worldwide (SUEZ worldwide, 2022a) and 
Water Vision Technology (Water Vision Technology, 2018) proposing 
and deploying synthetic aperture radar (SAR). Its use enables the 
identification of anomalies in soil moisture and dielectric properties, 
particularly in extensive or difficult-to-access regions without direct 
ground intervention. Despite the considerable spatial coverage advan-
tages offered by satellite monitoring, its accuracy may be affected by 
factors such as burial depth, soil composition, and environmental con-
ditions. Consequently, field validation is typically required to confirm 
the presence of leaks.
SUEZ worldwide (2022a), in a partnership with ASTERRA (SUEZ 
worldwide, 2022b), presented a series of favorable case studies using 
satellite technology. In Wisconsin Asterra (2021), satellite technology 
revealed 57 leaks in 2019 on 820 km of network compared to the 13 
leaks per year identified through traditional methods. This resulted in 
a reduction from 7% to 6.3% of the NRW, corresponding to a total 
decrease of 10%. On the other hand, the South Carolina (Asterra, 
2020a) case study achieved an improvement of 240% over conven-
tional methodologies by finding 44 leaks in around 215 km. Similar 
results are given by Water Vision Technology (2018), where this tech-
nology was applied to the GCC region (Water Vision Technology, 
2019), achieving in 79 days an accuracy of 89% in 6000 km of area 
covered.
In the field of integrating acoustic sensors with software analysis, 
numerous case studies have been conducted by FIDO Tech (2021). An 
example of a successful implementation was Northumbria, UK (FIDO 
Tech, 2023i,a), where 177 leaks across 470 km of metallic or plastic 
pipes were detected. The study found a reduction in leakage of more 
than 40%. Another case study, in Platte County, Missouri (FIDO Tech, 
2023f), demonstrated a 52% reduction, which corresponds to annual 
savings of 72 million liters, equivalent to financial savings of e90 
181. Finally, a case study in Bangkok, Thailand FIDO Tech (2023h) 
presented favorable outcomes in a low-pressure network with a noisy 
surrounding area.
Additionally, as demonstrated by the Xylem (2016) case study in 
Arkansas, USA (Xylem, 2024b), where with more than 30 acoustic 
sensors and a DMA analysis the NRW was reduced from 44% to 24%. 
Similarly, Veolia (2025a), a company with a greater number of case 
studies in France, has reported a significant improvement in leak detec-
tion through the use of smart meters. It identified over 300 leaks per 
week in the Lyon metropolitan region (Veolia, 2025b) and contributed 
to a reduction of 20% of leaks in Bordeaux (Veolia, 2024). Regarding 
the Badger Meter company (Badger-Meter, 2024a), which also uses 
ultrasonic and electromagnetic sensors, although their application area 
is limited to the USA, the implementation of these technologies has 
resulted in a reduction in the number of leaks. In the field of telemetry 
analysis, the efficacy of integrating acoustic sensors with these methods 
has been demonstrated by companies including HWM-Global (2016),

and reliable for precise localization. Conversely, smart metering and 
AI-based systems provide enhanced scalability and automation. Hy-

and analytical efficiency. Notwithstanding these advances, challenges 
regarding sensor density, data quality, operational costs, and transfer-

to fully scalable and universally applicable commercial solutions.
5. Industrial review: Registered patents
Regarding an industrial review, several patents exist for leakage 
detection and localization methods based on hardware-based, software-
based, and hybrid techniques. Table 8 provides a summary of the 
most relevant ones, from which can be highlighted CN-113775939-
B (Yuan and Pei, 2022), CN-115654381-A (Qinli et al., 2023), WO-
2017005269-A1 (Nielsen et al., 2017), BE-1029806-B1 (Van, 2023), 
and US-11494853-B2 (Tao et al., 2022). The aforementioned patents 
may be classified as hybrid methods, as they integrate sensor data with 
software-based approaches for data analysis, including hydraulic mod-
eling, pressure matrix techniques, statistical methods, and ML/ANNs. 
Additionally, some companies have also pursued patent protection for 
their methodology. TaKaDu, for instance, has been granted patents in a 
multitude of countries. Their patent portfolio includes patents related to 
data monitoring and statistical analysis, such as EP-2472467-B1 (Peleg 
et al., 2021), IE-86150-B1 (Armon et al., 2013), IE-86368-B1 (Pe-
leg et al., 2014b), US-9568392-B2 (Peleg et al., 2017), US-7920983-
B1 (Peleg et al., 2011b), AU-2011200949-B1 (Armon et al., 2011), 
GB2478432 A (Peleg et al., 2011a), GB-2499113-A (Peleg et al., 2013). 
TaKaDu has also patented technology for the localization of assets using 
GIS, as evidenced by patents US-9441988-B2 (Armon et al., 2016) and 
US-9053519-B2 (Scolnicov et al., 2015). The majority of the analyzed 
patents are predominantly classified as utility patents, as they pertain 
to functional inventions and methods. Therefore, the objective is to 
project features as methods, systems, devices, technical processes, and 
software with technical effects. Furthermore, it is possible to indirectly 
acknowledge the TRL (Technology Readiness Level) of each patent, 
with the higher technology maturity levels (TRL 6-7) attributed to the 
hardware-based solution, while software-based and hybrid approaches 
predominantly fall within TRL 5–7, with recent patent applications 
remaining at prototype or laboratory validation stages.
Fig. 17(a) shows that existing patents cover a range of leakage 
detection techniques, including hardware, software, and hybrid-based 
approaches, while Fig. 17(b) presents their yearly evolution from 2007 
to late 2023. Although software-based methods are the most pre-
dominant in the industrial review, hybrid-based methods emerged 
more prominently after 2021. This indicates a strong industry shift 
towards integrating hardware and software approaches, likely driven 
by the need for more sophisticated/effective solutions. Another impor-
tant point to highlight is that the total volume of patents registered 
in the last three years exceeds 50% of all other patents, underscoring 
the increasing interest in research on water leakage detection in recent 
years. It is also crucial to note that only patents with granted appli-
cations were considered in this review. This means that, on average, 
a minimum of 3 to 5 years typically passed from the initial patent 
application to its final issue to the applicant. Therefore, it can be 
concluded that the biggest boom in industrial patents likely began 
around 2016.
Fig. 18 presents a statistical analysis of the industrial review accord-
ing to the international patent classification. The analysis highlights 
a strong focus on the Physics category (68 patents), particularly in 
measuring and testing-related technologies (G01) with 30 patents and 
computing, calculating, and counting-related technologies (G06) with 
28 patents. G01 encompasses precision measurement tools and meth-
ods, including sensors and calibration techniques, while G06 covers 
hardware and software innovations in computing, data processing, 
and algorithmic calculations. These two categories represent over 65% 
of the total amount of patents, indicating a significant emphasis on 
technological advancements in these areas. Fixed Constructions has the 
least representation (6 patents) and includes technologies and methods 
related to building and infrastructure. It covers everything from water 
management systems and sewage networks to drilling techniques and 
mining operations.
6. Conclusions and future research directions
Leakage is a major problem, not only because it causes water 
loss, but also because it wastes the energy and chemicals used in 
treatment, creating significant financial costs. It can also harm the 
environment through the discharge of treated water and allow contam-
inants to enter the network, posing risks to human health (Z. Hu et al., 
2021). These impacts reinforce the urgency of developing reliable, 
scalable, and scientifically grounded leakage detection and localization 
methodologies.
In light of this critical concern, this study presented a compre-
hensive and multidisciplinary review of water leakage detection and 
localization within WSS, offering a critical synthesis across scientific, 
commercial, and industrial perspectives. It systematically compares 
hardware-based, model-based, data-driven, and hybrid approaches un-
der real-world operational constraints, trade-offs and their practical 
applicability, including scalability, uncertainty propagation, and data 
dependency. The review shows a clear shift toward hybrid solutions 
as promising scalable and resilient strategies for leak detection, largely 
driven by the growing use of ML techniques in water leak detection and 
localization in water supply systems. These techniques have demon-
strated strong potential for capturing complex, nonlinear relationships

in monitoring data, although their performance remains highly depen-

the scientific literature further reveals that many proposed methodolo-
gies are validated under idealized or benchmark conditions, with lim-
ited transferability to real networks affected by sensor noise, demand 
uncertainty, and incomplete system knowledge. Although promising 
detection accuracies are frequently reported, comparative assessments 
across studies are hindered by the lack of standardized datasets, evalu-
ation metrics, and experimental protocols. This limitation underscores 
the need for reproducible research practices and open benchmarking 
frameworks within the scientific community. The benchmark presented 
highlights the diversity of approaches, from purely data-driven to hy-
brid and model-based solutions, suggesting that combining hydraulic 
modeling with advanced analytics can improve performance, a relevant 
topic in the field of smart water systems and infrastructure monitoring.
On the other hand, the commercial review offers an overview 
of commercial techniques and technologies used for leak detection 
and localization in WSS, for understanding the current technological 
availability and market trends. This analysis highlights that commer-
cial solutions still rely predominantly on traditional hardware-based 
methods, such as acoustic sensors, which require manual operation, 
are time-intensive, and depend substantially on operator expertise. By 
contrast, hybrid solutions aim to integrate the strengths of hardware-
based approaches with software-based analytical methods to enhance 
overall performance. Companies like FIDO Tech, TaKaDu, SUEZ, and 
HWM Global, among others demonstrate the growing impact of AI and 
remote sensing technologies in the sector. These solutions have led to 
measurable improvements in leak detection speed and cost savings.
Meanwhile, the industrial review summarized important patents 
related to leakage detection in WSS and notes a recent surge, espe-
cially after 2021, in hybrid solutions that combine sensor data with 
software techniques like ML, statistical analysis, and hydraulic model-
ing. Companies like TaKaDu are highlighted for their active patenting 
in data monitoring and GIS-based asset localization. In addition, a 
granular analysis of patent classifications reveals a strong emphasis on 
technological advancements within precision measurement tools, data 
processing algorithms, and computing innovations in shaping the future 
of water leakage detection.
In conclusion, there is no ideal method for the detection and local-
ization process as it depends on the system’s characterization (network 
length, elements, ageing, material, among others), available informa-
tion (pressure and demands data), and possible approaches using ML 
models. The insights presented here provide a way for future research 
to prioritize underexplored domains to address global water leakage 
challenges. As part of the authors’ future work, the potential for a 
hybrid system combining hardware-based technologies with software-
based analysis to improve accuracy and reliability will be investigated. 
Moreover, as a future research direction, the authors pinpoint that the 
application of ML and physics-informed models to WSS should be sub-
jected to further analysis for detection and localization purposes, with 
the PINN model approach being capable of providing information at 
strategic points following physical governance laws. These approaches 
can be tested in well-known benchmarks and real network case scenar-
ios. Further research may be conducted on the calibration of sensors, 
with the objective of evaluating their reliability and understanding how 
they affect the measurements used to detect and localize water leaks.
